title: American views of China remain more negative than positive but have warmed since 2021
source_unit: Pew Research Center American Trends Panel feeling-thermometer survey of U.S. adults

observations.period: 2016, 2018, 2021, and September 14-20, 2026 survey comparison; report September 23, 2026

denominator.unit: U.S. adults who rated China in the 2026 four-country feeling-thermometer module; full panel survey n=5193

2026_distribution.unit: percent of U.S. adults rating China

change_since_2021.value: warm views +8 points; neutral views +7 points; cold views -14 points; average rating +9 points

subgroup_pattern.value: Democrats and younger adults give warmer ratings than Republicans and older adults

observations.method: American Trends Panel survey conducted September 14-20, 2026; each respondent rated four of 18 countries on a 0-100 feeling thermometer, with China-rated respondents forming the analytic subset.
observations.uncertainty: The 2026 estimate is a cross-sectional survey comparison with different module routing and sample sizes across years. A warmer rating does not establish support for Chinese policy, reduced security concern, trade preference, or changed political behavior.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with comparisons by party and age; the published analytic subset rated China in the randomized country module.
observations.counterinterpretation: Sentiment can warm while strategic distrust, policy disagreement, or views of Chinese government remain negative. Changes may also reflect question context, current events, or cohort composition rather than a durable realignment.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. public-attitude time trend toward China. It does not infer alliance change, threat reduction, policy support, economic dependence, or future diplomatic behavior from thermometer ratings.
